recent_posts.title: Why secrets management is incomplete without secret scanning
recent_posts.summary: Secret scanning complements traditional secrets management by discovering hidden credentials scattered across code repositories, pipelines, and infrastructure. While platforms like HashiCorp Vault secure known secrets, scanning tools like Vault Radar provide visibility into unmanaged secrets that attackers actively target. A complete secrets lifecycle strategy combines detection, notification, import, cleanup, and rotation to create continuous protection. Organizations typically take 94 days to remediate leaked secrets, making real-time detection crucial for reducing attack surface and maintaining compliance.

recent_posts.title: 4 security wins from Booking.com's hybrid cloud migration
recent_posts.summary: Booking.com successfully scaled HashiCorp Vault to handle 500+ requests per second across 100+ Kubernetes clusters during their hybrid cloud migration. Their approach created a unified security bridge between multi-cloud environments, consolidated authentication complexity through JWT migration, implemented strategic cloud-native secrets management with Vault as single source of truth, and maintained cost-effective operations. The solution enabled self-service developer onboarding while maintaining security oversight across AWS, GCP, Alibaba Cloud, and bare metal infrastructure.

recent_posts.title: Five best practices for multi cloud credential management
recent_posts.summary: Platform engineer Lino Telera shares five best practices for managing credentials across multi-cloud environments: replacing static API keys with dynamic secrets, automating runtime secret management, implementing workspace sandboxing for zero trust, centralizing infrastructure templates, and using bootstrap templates for rapid deployment. These approaches reduce operational overhead, improve security, and enable developer autonomy while maintaining consistent security practices across teams and environments.

recent_posts.title: Policy as code, explained
recent_posts.summary: Policy as code automates IT requirement enforcement by codifying policies that can be tested, versioned, and automatically applied to infrastructure deployments. This approach replaces manual document-based policy reviews with automated checks that provide instant feedback, reducing deployment times from weeks to minutes while maintaining security, compliance, and cost controls. The framework enables developer self-service while ensuring guardrails are maintained through readable policy languages like Sentinel.

recent_posts.title: Terraform provider for Google Cloud 7.0 is now GA
recent_posts.summary: HashiCorp released version 7.0 of the Terraform Google Cloud provider with enhanced security features including ephemeral resources for temporary credentials and write-only attributes for sensitive data. The update introduces improved validation logic, API alignment changes, and breaking changes that require configuration updates. Key security improvements prevent sensitive data like passwords and access tokens from being stored in Terraform state files.

recent_posts.title: Secret sprawl costs organizations millions in lost developer productivity
recent_posts.summary: Secret sprawl, the uncontrolled spread of credentials across development tools and repositories, costs organizations significant money through reduced productivity. A typical 50-person development team loses $936,000 annually on secret-related tasks like hunting exposed credentials, rotating keys, and debugging failed deployments. Security teams waste an additional $520,000 investigating false positive alerts. Beyond direct costs, secret sprawl creates hidden velocity taxes through development delays, context switching, and tool fragmentation that erode competitive advantage.

recent_posts.title: Why default secret detection rules don't work (and how to fix it)
recent_posts.summary: Default secret detection tools generate up to 80% false positives while missing organization-specific credentials. Context-aware scanning solutions like HCP Vault Radar address this by offering custom regex patterns, severity-based prioritization, global ignore rules, and intelligent filtering. These features reduce noise, improve detection accuracy for proprietary secrets, and enable automated workflows that route critical issues appropriately while keeping teams focused on real threats.

recent_posts.title: How to enable developer self-service at scale with Terraform and Waypoint
recent_posts.summary: Platform teams can enable developer self-service at scale by combining HCP Waypoint with Terraform no-code modules. The approach involves creating reusable infrastructure templates that abstract complex Terraform configurations, allowing developers to provision resources through a simplified interface while maintaining organizational guardrails. The workflow includes setting up HCP Terraform projects with proper credentials, bootstrapping EKS clusters, creating no-code modules, and building Waypoint templates that developers can use without deep infrastructure expertise. This combination provides speed with security through automated provisioning, policy enforcement, and audit trails.

recent_posts.title: How Moneybox scaled from 3 to 75 engineers using HCP Terraform
recent_posts.summary: Moneybox, a UK fintech managing £15 billion in assets, successfully migrated from Terraform Community Edition to HCP Terraform to address scaling challenges. The transition eliminated CI/CD maintenance overhead, enabled self-service infrastructure for 75 engineers across 90+ workspaces, and implemented governance workflows required for regulatory compliance. Key lessons include starting simple but recognizing when to scale, designing infrastructure for growth, building reliable self-service capabilities, integrating governance into workflows, and maintaining balance between speed and structure.

recent_posts.title: Terraform now supports assigning agent pools at the project level
recent_posts.summary: HCP Terraform and Terraform Enterprise now allow users to assign default agent pools at the project level, replacing the previous workspace-only configuration. This enhancement improves scalability and reduces manual configuration overhead by automatically applying agent pool settings to new workspaces within a project. Project owners can set default execution modes, while workspace admins retain the ability to override settings for specific requirements. The feature addresses previous limitations around time-consuming, error-prone manual agent pool assignments and provides a more self-service approach to infrastructure management.
